top_choice_rationale: Optical lattice clocks (Katori and Ye) rest on a distinct physical idea, the magic-wavelength lattice that cancels the differential light shift so many atoms can be interrogated at once, and the resulting 10^-18 performance has been reproduced and intercompared across independent laboratories for over a decade. That is the maturity and robustness test I trust most. The two-name allocation is the cleanest on the slate, with every opening ballot proposing the same pair, and the citation can be anchored on the lattice concept and its realisation, not on records, which limits overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes. Magic-angle graphene is a strong theory-experiment chain but is eight years old with an open pairing mechanism and an exposed credit boundary (Cao, Dean group, earlier twisted-bilayer theory); topological insulators are mature but the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio omits the 3D branch and overlaps with the 2016 prize. A prize is still preferable to no award.
recusal_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work on superconducting circuits, so I would recuse myself on circuit QED (B021), which is not on the proposal slate. No tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp is apparent from my profile.
